en: The Scripture on the Ground of the Small Path, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Yao of India during the Later Han Dynasty.
Regarding why a practitioner of the Way who seeks stillness fails to attain it, there are four causes and conditions. What are they?
What are the four?
First, relying on what is good, one does not understand how to protect the precepts for the sake of one's own body;

second, because one does not protect the precepts, cleverness of mind does not arise; because cleverness of mind does not arise, one does not know the body; and because one does not know the body, the mind becomes deluded.
Third, they do not understand the sutras; because they do not understand the sutras, they lack clarity; because they lack clarity, their minds become doubtful.
Fourth, they do not frequently calculate that their lifespan and merit are daily diminishing, yet their minds remain complacent.
Because of these four causes and conditions, one cannot attain stillness.
When a practitioner seeks stillness and desires to attain it, they must understand two matters regarding sitting and walking:
first, panting; [second, gasping].
Second is cessation (*nirodha*).
It also depends on two causes and conditions:
first, for the sake of arising; [second, for the sake of abiding].
Second, it is for death.
What is panting? What is breathing?
The arising of the mind is panting; the ceasing of the mind is stillness.
What is birth? What is death?
The cessation of the mind is birth; the arising of the mind is death.
One must first understand that these are dependent origination; one should then be able to discern and know from where this dependent origination arises and ceases.
The matter lies in four pairs. What are the four?
First, not knowing moderation in eating, eating excessively, failing to train oneself, and failing to exercise restraint, resulting in greed for flavors beyond sufficiency;
Second, the mind follows after forms; failing to examine them with discernment, one pursues many personal desires, which constitutes the root of suffering.
Third, the hindrance of mental agitation arises; one sleeps excessively, loses fundamental mindfulness, and plants the seeds for dreams.
Fourth, doubt and evil increase daily; one engages in double-tongued speech, falls into error, and gives rise to false anger, such that body and speech are no longer in accord.
For this reason, one does not fall away from dhyāna; how then could one fail to draw near to it?

Constantly and repeatedly contemplating the arising and ceasing, the rising and passing away of the breath—what kind of mental intention should one maintain to perform such contemplation and discernment?
It also depends on four causes and conditions:
first, associating with virtuous friends;
second, understanding and accepting their words without falsehood.
Third, one should greedily recite the sutras, training the mind day and night;
fourth, one should guard the precepts and never depart from the Dharma.
Thus, tranquility is easily attained.
The body has four ailments:
at times earth is excessive, and the body finds no peace;
at times water is excessive, and the body finds no peace.
At times when fire is excessive, the body finds no peace;
at times when wind is excessive, the body finds no peace.
Only when these four elements attain equilibrium does the body find rest.
The mind has four ailments:
first, when delusion is excessive, the mind cannot find stillness;
second, when hatred is excessive, the mind cannot find stillness.
Third, when lust is excessive, the mind cannot find rest;
fourth, when doubt is excessive, the mind cannot find rest.
When these four matters are unsettled, the mind cannot find rest.
The breath also has four ailments:
at times one seeks too much and the breath cannot be stilled;
at times one’s thoughts are too numerous and the breath cannot be stilled.
At times, when joy is excessive, the breath cannot be stilled;
at other times, when panting is excessive, the breath cannot be stilled.
When a practitioner of the Way walks the path, by departing from these causes and conditions, they attain a concentrated mind.
If the body is swollen with goiters, scabies, or sores, or is excessively corpulent, one cannot find peace when sitting;
or if at times one eats too much, fire arises within and the body finds no peace;
or if at times one drinks too much, water arises within, the body becomes heavy and the eyes blurred, and the body finds no peace.

Or at times, having already eaten much, one eats again, greedily overindulging in flavors; failing to train oneself and lacking restraint, wind arises so that one cannot find peace, and this is also called "eating too little."

If one has an abundance of delusion, it is not appropriate to frequently enter among the crowds of people; one should first recite the sutras, and rather than seeking extensive learning, one should prefer self-restraint.
If one has an abundance of anger and hatred, it is not appropriate to live at home or to possess few belongings.
If lust is excessive, one should not view performances, music, or various beautiful forms.

If doubt is excessive, one should not frequently listen to pleasant words or eloquent speech, but should always maintain self-restraint, engage in contemplation, and subject oneself to critical examination.
If one seeks much, one should constantly maintain mindfulness of impermanence, attending to it whether sitting or rising.
If one’s thoughts are many, one should always practice to realize that all that I have thought of is the root of suffering.
If joy is excessive, it will not last long; suffering will follow later, and one must restrain it through illness.
If sighing and lamentation are excessive, one should always harmonize the mind and should not frequently utter coarse words, thereby committing offenses while sitting.
When a practitioner of the Way walks the path, if they do not recognize these causes and conditions, they will ultimately never draw near to the Way.
One should be able to restrain this; as wise discernment gradually increases, the Way becomes easy to attain.
When a practitioner of the Way seeks to advance toward the Way, they must understand that past thoughts and matters have already passed and should no longer be dwelt upon.
Why is this? It is because one further understands it as a seed.
For example, when sowing grain, if one sows rice, one thinks, "I shall reap rice"; if one sows beans, one thinks, "I shall reap beans."
Why is this? Because they arise. Recollection is likewise:

by planting the seeds of recollection, they arise; all these aggregates exist throughout the ten directions, awaiting calamity or merit to receive their karmic requital, and thus cannot escape suffering.

Falling into killing is the planting of killing; planting theft is the planting of theft; planting sexual misconduct is the planting of sexual misconduct; planting double-tongued speech is the planting of double-tongued speech; planting harsh speech is the planting of harsh speech; planting false speech is the planting of false speech; planting frivolous speech is the planting of frivolous speech; planting envy is the planting of envy; planting malice is the planting of malice; planting doubt is the planting of doubt. Planting is the act of sowing.
Therefore, one should repeatedly cultivate mindfulness and further increase it; for it is difficult to attain liberation from suffering.
By what means should one abandon these manifold sufferings?
One must abandon them through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), so as not to plant these ten non-virtuous actions again; though other seeds may remain, they will eventually be exhausted.

Why is this? It is like planting grain: although one may obtain a great harvest, if one does not sow again but merely eats from it little by little, even though one eats for a long time without ceasing, there will eventually come a time when it is exhausted.
The same applies to the abandonment through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Why is this?
Because [the seeds] are no longer sown.
By abandoning through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one's offenses gradually diminish. Why is this?
Because abandoning through meditative concentration constitutes merit; as merit arises, all evils come to an end.
One merely plants the seeds of the thought of the Way; once the Way has arisen, there is wisdom (*prajñā*). Possessing wisdom, one can sustain others and also sustain oneself.

When a practitioner of the Way seeks to advance toward the Buddha-way and desires to clearly understand and know the workings of the mind in this present life, the essentials lie in three types of mindfulness:
past mindfulness, future mindfulness, and present mindfulness.
There are thoughts of merit and thoughts of demerit.

At times, while reciting the scriptures or practicing meditation, one suddenly recalls a long-past event of being insulted by others, or of having harmed someone or fallen into lustful desires. Because of these recollections, mental formations arise, which then develop into heads and feet [i.e., full physical actions]; thus, one’s transgressions increase beyond control. From these causes and conditions, one incurs demerit, which becomes the root of suffering; this is what is meant by thoughts of past demerit.

At times, while in meditative concentration or reading the scriptures, a wholesome thought may suddenly arise; one recollects the suffering and pleasure experienced during past practices and contemplates that these are not permanent. This is called the mindfulness of past merit.
At times when one is at peace, if a sudden distracted thought arises and one contemplates impermanence, one then loses the original mindfulness.
When greed and lust lead to excessive seeking, one then forms the thought of immortality; this constitutes a future sinful thought.
At times, if one attains tranquility, one should skillfully plant the seeds of mindfulness; through these causes and conditions, wisdom will increase—this is the mindfulness of future merit.

If one lives as a layperson, maintaining self-restraint and observing the precepts, yet wrong thoughts arise, one should reflect: "To keep many domestic animals increases anxiety and leads to the loss of the precepts"—this is the mindfulness of present demerit.
To dwell in one's own home while personally maintaining the precepts, further increasing wholesome thoughts and constantly desiring detachment—this is the merit and mindfulness of the present.
Those who seek the path of the Buddha should first understand these matters of transgression and merit; only then can their wisdom increase.
If one seeks arhatship through the total severance of all [defilements], this constitutes seeking the path toward Buddhahood.
However, if one seeks arhatship merely to increase merit and cultivate wisdom, or seeks it merely to fall into dhyāna and extinguish evil, such wisdom remains secondary.
Those who seek to become Buddhas and increase their merit must be extensively learned;
those who seek wisdom must recite the sutras.

If one wishes to know the essential point, it lies in guarding the precepts. By guarding the precepts, one can then understand the sutras, bring blessings to others, and likewise bring blessings to oneself.
A practitioner who seeks to advance toward the Buddha-way and wishes to understand the intent of the bodhisattva practice in this present life must further know these three precepts:
first, one should know that upholding the precepts also involves guarding them;
second, one should know that not violating the precepts also involves being able to exercise restraint.
Third, one should know that there are the precepts, the awakening to the precepts, the ability to observe the precepts, and the protection of the precepts.

First, regarding what is to be known as "upholding the precepts": if a person has a wife and children and, while living at home, constantly observes the fasts without fail, this is called upholding the precepts;
if one has no wife or children and maintains oneself without inclining toward the improper, this is called guarding the precepts.

Second, one should know that not violating the precepts means that if a person sees with the eyes or hears with the ears, they are able to remain undisturbed by sounds and forms, as well as all other sensory objects; this is what constitutes not violating the precepts.

To undergo the hardships of cold for the sake of the Way, and yet, when insulted by others, not lose one's original mindfulness—this is called enduring the precepts, and one should likewise practice patience.
Third, one should know the precepts: knowing that a certain person maintains a certain precept is what constitutes knowing the precepts.

Regarding "instructing on the precepts": if one knows that a certain person delights in the Path but is disparaged and envied by their parents, kinsmen, and acquaintances, one should not frequently instruct them on the precepts in the midst of a large assembly.

Regarding "being able to observe the precepts": one should know that according to what kind of karma a person is suited for, one bestows upon them [the training] according to their capacity; this enables them not to lose it. Whether increasing or decreasing [the practice], one administers medicine according to the illness—this is called being able to observe the precepts.

Regarding the protection of the precepts: one should protect them all; one should accord with and follow their intent; one should maintain a protective resolve to distance oneself from evil associates; and one desires to speak of the humans and non-humans of the ten directions.

Whether amidst music and entertainment or amidst sensual desires, if one can teach others to speak many virtuous words, maintain an undisturbed mind, and further cause them to gain merit, this is called guarding the precepts.

Those who seek to follow the bodhisattva path and practice its deeds must understand this; only then can they liberate others while liberating themselves, and bring others to spiritual maturity while bringing themselves to maturity.
The Sūtra on the Stages of the Lesser Path Spoken by the Buddha
